title: UPSC Law MCQ Question Bank
description: Lex Academy interactive MCQ bank aligned to the UPSC Civil Services Law Optional syllabus. Questions tagged as UPSC Prelims PYQ - adapted are paraphrased from law/polity questions appearing in Civil Services Preliminary Examination GS papers; other questions are independently written from primary legal materials.
methodology: Scope follows the UPSC Law Optional syllabus: Constitutional & Administrative Law and International Law in Paper I; Crimes, Torts, Contracts/Mercantile Law and Contemporary Legal Developments in Paper II.
Previous UPSC Prelims questions are adapted/paraphrased rather than reproduced wholesale. Their exam year is stored in previousExamYear and the source type is marked UPSC Prelims PYQ - adapted.
Explanations are independently written for Lex Academy.
Current-law questions use current statutory frameworks where appropriate, including BNS, BNSS and BSA. Historical PYQ adaptations retain the context relevant to their examination year.
This bank is an educational practice resource and should be periodically reviewed when statutes, rules or leading judgments change.

questions.explanation: A Money Bill cannot be introduced in Rajya Sabha. The Council may recommend changes within fourteen days, but Lok Sabha may accept or reject them.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: How many Delimitation Commissions had been constituted in India up to December 2023?
questions.explanation: Four Delimitation Commissions had been constituted: in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The 71st Constitutional Amendment added which set of languages to the Eighth Schedule?
questions.explanation: The 71st Amendment added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali to the Eighth Schedule.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Municipalities are governed by Part IXA; emergency provisions are in Part XVIII and amendment provisions in Part XX.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which subject is in the Union List?
questions.explanation: Inter-State quarantine is a Union List subject. Public order, police and agriculture are principally State List subjects.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The Supreme Court located the constitutional right to privacy primarily within:
options: Article 21 read with the freedoms in Part III
questions.explanation: Puttaswamy recognised privacy as protected under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms and dignity protected by Part III.
questions.reference: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: A demand for a grant in Parliament can be made only on the recommendation of:
questions.explanation: Article 113 requires that no demand for a grant be made except on the recommendation of the President.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: While a resolution for removal of the Lok Sabha Speaker is under consideration, the Speaker:
options: May preside and cast a deciding vote only
Shall not preside but may speak and vote in the first instance
questions.explanation: Article 96 bars the Speaker from presiding during consideration of a removal resolution, but permits participation and a vote in the first instance.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which bill lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
options: A bill pending only in Rajya Sabha and not passed by Lok Sabha
A bill passed by Lok Sabha and pending in Rajya Sabha
A bill for which a joint sitting has already been notified
A Constitutional Amendment Bill pending in Rajya Sabha only
questions.explanation: A bill originating in and passed by Lok Sabha but pending in Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution. A bill pending in Rajya Sabha that has not been passed by Lok Sabha does not.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: In constitutional discourse, 'due process of law' most strongly conveys:
options: Purely formal enactment of any procedure
Fairness and natural justice in the application of law
questions.explanation: Due process goes beyond bare formal procedure and incorporates substantive and procedural fairness.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The chief purpose of a Constitution is best described as:
options: Defining and limiting governmental power while structuring institutions
questions.explanation: A constitution creates governmental institutions, allocates powers and imposes limits on public authority.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which amendment is historically associated with responding to early judicial interpretations of Fundamental Rights?
questions.explanation: The First Amendment, 1951 introduced changes including Article 19(2), Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule in response to early constitutional litigation.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Who declares an area to be a Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule?
questions.explanation: The President may declare areas to be Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Article 335 is principally concerned with:
options: Claims of SCs and STs to services and posts consistently with administrative efficiency
questions.explanation: Article 335 addresses the claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to services and posts, consistent with maintenance of administrative efficiency.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Rajya Sabha's constitutional role on a Money Bill is to:
questions.explanation: Rajya Sabha may recommend amendments but cannot amend or reject a Money Bill; Lok Sabha decides whether to accept recommendations.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: The Constitution itself defines civil and criminal contempt
Supreme Court and High Courts are courts of record with contempt powers
Parliament has no legislative competence concerning contempt
Only subordinate courts may punish contempt
questions.explanation: Articles 129 and 215 recognise the Supreme Court and High Courts as courts of record with contempt powers; statutory definitions are in the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which power is exclusive to the Lok Sabha?
options: Passing a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers
questions.explanation: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, so a no-confidence motion operates there.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Under the Tenth Schedule, a nominated member may join a political party without disqualification if the joining occurs:
options: Within six months of taking the seat
questions.explanation: A nominated member may join a political party within six months of taking the seat without attracting disqualification on that ground.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: A key protective consequence of Fifth Schedule governance is that it can support:
options: Conversion of Scheduled Areas into Union Territories
Restrictions protecting tribal land from transfer to non-tribals
Direct rule by Parliament in every case
questions.explanation: The Fifth Schedule framework permits special laws and regulations protecting tribal interests, including restrictions on transfer of tribal land.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Unguided and uncontrolled discretionary power conferred on the executive is most directly vulnerable under:
questions.explanation: Arbitrary or unguided discretion can offend the equality and non-arbitrariness principle under Article 14.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The constitutional status of the right to property in India is:
options: Constitutional/legal right available to persons under Article 300A
questions.explanation: After the 44th Amendment, property ceased to be a Fundamental Right but is protected by Article 300A, available to 'no person' except by authority of law.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Abolition of untouchability falls within which broad Fundamental Right category?
questions.explanation: Article 17 is located within the Right to Equality cluster in Part III.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which Part of the Constitution most directly expresses the ideal of a welfare State through non-justiciable governance principles?
questions.explanation: Part IV contains the Directive Principles of State Policy, which guide the State toward social and economic welfare.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Audi alteram partem'?
options: law made by an authority under power conferred by a parent statute
the rule that a person should not be condemned unheard
a specialised adjudicatory body created by law to decide specified disputes
questions.explanation: It is a core limb of natural justice requiring a fair opportunity of hearing.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Nemo judex in causa sua'?
options: legislation complete in itself that leaves to another authority the determination of when, where or to whom it will apply
constitutional supervision of legality rather than a general appeal on merits
questions.explanation: No person should judge a cause in which he or she has an interest.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Speaking order'?
options: a tribunal dealing primarily with service matters of specified public servants
an order that records reasons for the decision
a classic form of disqualifying bias
constitutional provision enabling Parliament to establish administrative tribunals for service matters
questions.explanation: Reasoned decisions improve fairness, accountability and facilitate judicial review.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Delegated legislation'?
options: a classic form of disqualifying bias
a procedural or sometimes substantive expectation created by consistent representation or practice of public authority
a writ requiring justification of a person's detention
law made by an authority under power conferred by a parent statute
questions.explanation: Delegated legislation derives validity from the enabling Act and must remain within its limits.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Ultra vires'?
options: constitutional provision enabling Parliament to establish administrative tribunals for service matters
administrative or delegated action beyond legal power
a writ requiring justification of a person's detention
an ombudsman institution generally operating at the State level under State law
questions.explanation: Action outside statutory or constitutional authority is liable to be struck down as ultra vires.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Wednesbury unreasonableness'?
options: review of a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it
a classic form of disqualifying bias
a provision authorising delegated legislation to modify provisions of the parent Act or other primary legislation
a doctrine preventing a public authority in appropriate cases from resiling from a clear promise relied upon
questions.explanation: The doctrine is associated with Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corporation.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Proportionality'?
options: a doctrine preventing a public authority in appropriate cases from resiling from a clear promise relied upon
review asking whether a rights-restricting measure is suitably tailored and no more restrictive than justified
a duty owed under public law that can support remedies such as mandamus
questions.explanation: Proportionality is increasingly used in constitutional and administrative review.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Legitimate expectation'?
options: a procedural or sometimes substantive expectation created by consistent representation or practice of public authority
review of a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it
exercise of power for an improper purpose or in bad faith
questions.explanation: It protects fairness where public conduct creates a reasonable expectation, subject to public interest.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Promissory estoppel'?
options: a doctrine preventing a public authority in appropriate cases from resiling from a clear promise relied upon
the rule that a person should not be condemned unheard
the idea that content of fair procedure depends on context, statute and consequences
questions.explanation: The doctrine can apply against government subject to statutory limits and overriding public interest.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Malafides'?
options: a procedural or sometimes substantive expectation created by consistent representation or practice of public authority
a provision authorising delegated legislation to modify provisions of the parent Act or other primary legislation
a writ restraining a lower court or tribunal from continuing proceedings without or in excess of jurisdiction
exercise of power for an improper purpose or in bad faith
questions.explanation: Mala fide exercise of statutory power is a recognised ground of judicial review.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Relevant considerations'?
options: the requirement that a statutory authority consider legally relevant matters and ignore irrelevant ones
administrative or delegated action beyond legal power
review asking whether a rights-restricting measure is suitably tailored and no more restrictive than justified
a doctrine preventing a public authority in appropriate cases from resiling from a clear promise relied upon
questions.explanation: Failure to consider relevant factors or reliance on irrelevant factors can invalidate administrative action.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Sub-delegation'?
options: an ombudsman institution generally operating at the State level under State law
a procedural or sometimes substantive expectation created by consistent representation or practice of public authority
a writ requiring justification of a person's detention
questions.explanation: A delegate ordinarily cannot sub-delegate unless the parent law permits it: delegatus non potest delegare.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Henry VIII clause'?
options: legislation complete in itself that leaves to another authority the determination of when, where or to whom it will apply
a classic form of disqualifying bias
a provision authorising delegated legislation to modify provisions of the parent Act or other primary legislation
questions.explanation: Such clauses attract close scrutiny because they enlarge executive law-making power.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Conditional legislation'?
options: a specialised adjudicatory body created by law to decide specified disputes
a provision authorising delegated legislation to modify provisions of the parent Act or other primary legislation
a writ requiring justification of a person's detention
legislation complete in itself that leaves to another authority the determination of when, where or to whom it will apply
questions.explanation: It differs from delegated legislation in the nature of discretion left to the executive.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Administrative tribunal'?
options: a doctrine preventing a public authority in appropriate cases from resiling from a clear promise relied upon
a specialised adjudicatory body created by law to decide specified disputes
administrative or delegated action beyond legal power
questions.explanation: Tribunals exercise adjudicatory functions but remain subject to constitutional judicial review.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Lokpal'?
options: an ombudsman institution generally operating at the State level under State law
the principle under Article 310 that civil posts are held during the pleasure of the President or Governor, subject to constitutional safeguards
a tribunal dealing primarily with service matters of specified public servants
a statutory anti-corruption ombudsman at the Union level
questions.explanation: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 establishes the Lokpal.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Lokayukta'?
options: an ombudsman institution generally operating at the State level under State law
a procedural or sometimes substantive expectation created by consistent representation or practice of public authority
the rule that a person should not be condemned unheard
constitutional supervision of legality rather than a general appeal on merits
questions.explanation: Lokayukta structures differ across States.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Central Administrative Tribunal'?
options: a statutory anti-corruption ombudsman at the Union level
the idea that content of fair procedure depends on context, statute and consequences
a writ questioning the authority by which a person holds a public office
a tribunal dealing primarily with service matters of specified public servants
questions.explanation: The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 provides the statutory framework.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Doctrine of pleasure'?
options: a statutory anti-corruption ombudsman at the Union level
the principle under Article 310 that civil posts are held during the pleasure of the President or Governor, subject to constitutional safeguards
constitutional provision enabling Parliament to establish administrative tribunals for service matters
a hearing afforded after an urgent administrative decision
questions.explanation: Article 311 provides procedural protections against dismissal, removal or reduction in rank for covered civil servants.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Article 311'?
options: constitutional safeguards to specified civil servants against dismissal, removal or reduction in rank
constitutional provision enabling tribunals for specified subject matters beyond service matters
a specialised adjudicatory body created by law to decide specified disputes
questions.explanation: It ordinarily requires an inquiry and reasonable opportunity, subject to constitutional exceptions.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Article 323A'?
options: an ombudsman institution generally operating at the State level under State law
a procedural or sometimes substantive expectation created by consistent representation or practice of public authority
a tribunal dealing primarily with service matters of specified public servants
constitutional provision enabling Parliament to establish administrative tribunals for service matters
questions.explanation: Article 323A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Article 323B'?
options: constitutional provision enabling tribunals for specified subject matters beyond service matters
an order that records reasons for the decision
a duty owed under public law that can support remedies such as mandamus
a writ requiring justification of a person's detention
questions.explanation: Article 323B authorises legislatures to create tribunals for listed matters.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Certiorari'?
options: an ombudsman institution generally operating at the State level under State law
review of a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it
a writ used to quash an order of an inferior court, tribunal or authority for jurisdictional or legal error
the idea that content of fair procedure depends on context, statute and consequences
questions.explanation: Certiorari is corrective and supervisory in nature.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Prohibition'?
options: the idea that content of fair procedure depends on context, statute and consequences
constitutional provision enabling tribunals for specified subject matters beyond service matters
a statutory anti-corruption ombudsman at the Union level
a writ restraining a lower court or tribunal from continuing proceedings without or in excess of jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Prohibition operates prospectively to stop unlawful proceedings.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Mandamus'?
options: bias arising from structural or organisational interests rather than personal prejudice
a classic form of disqualifying bias
a writ requiring justification of a person's detention
a writ commanding performance of a public or statutory duty
questions.explanation: Mandamus generally lies to compel performance of a public duty.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Quo warranto'?
options: a doctrine preventing a public authority in appropriate cases from resiling from a clear promise relied upon
a writ questioning the authority by which a person holds a public office
the requirement that a statutory authority consider legally relevant matters and ignore irrelevant ones
the rule that a person should not be condemned unheard
questions.explanation: Quo warranto protects against unlawful occupation of a public office.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Habeas corpus'?
options: legislation complete in itself that leaves to another authority the determination of when, where or to whom it will apply
a writ requiring justification of a person's detention
constitutional provision enabling tribunals for specified subject matters beyond service matters
a writ restraining a lower court or tribunal from continuing proceedings without or in excess of jurisdiction
questions.explanation: It is a principal judicial remedy against unlawful detention.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Natural justice flexibility'?
options: a tribunal dealing primarily with service matters of specified public servants
an ombudsman institution generally operating at the State level under State law
the idea that content of fair procedure depends on context, statute and consequences
questions.explanation: Natural justice is not a rigid code; its requirements vary with the decision-making context.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Post-decisional hearing'?
options: a hearing afforded after an urgent administrative decision
a specialised adjudicatory body created by law to decide specified disputes
a writ restraining a lower court or tribunal from continuing proceedings without or in excess of jurisdiction
questions.explanation: It may cure procedural fairness in limited contexts but is not a universal substitute for prior hearing.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Bias from pecuniary interest'?
options: a specialised adjudicatory body created by law to decide specified disputes
bias arising from structural or organisational interests rather than personal prejudice
a duty owed under public law that can support remedies such as mandamus
a classic form of disqualifying bias
questions.explanation: Even a small direct financial interest may create disqualification in adjudicatory decision-making.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Institutional bias'?
options: a procedural or sometimes substantive expectation created by consistent representation or practice of public authority
bias arising from structural or organisational interests rather than personal prejudice
the principle under Article 310 that civil posts are held during the pleasure of the President or Governor, subject to constitutional safeguards
a writ questioning the authority by which a person holds a public office
questions.explanation: Administrative design may be challenged where institutional arrangements compromise impartiality.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Exclusion of natural justice'?
options: administrative or delegated action beyond legal power
constitutional supervision of legality rather than a general appeal on merits
a classic form of disqualifying bias
questions.explanation: Courts generally construe exclusion narrowly, especially where serious civil consequences follow.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Judicial review'?
options: a writ commanding performance of a public or statutory duty
constitutional supervision of legality rather than a general appeal on merits
a writ questioning the authority by which a person holds a public office
a procedural or sometimes substantive expectation created by consistent representation or practice of public authority
questions.explanation: Review focuses on legality, rationality, procedural fairness and constitutional limits.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Administrative discretion'?
options: choice legally entrusted to an authority within statutory boundaries
a writ used to quash an order of an inferior court, tribunal or authority for jurisdictional or legal error
administrative or delegated action beyond legal power
an ombudsman institution generally operating at the State level under State law
questions.explanation: Discretion must be exercised for proper purpose, on relevant grounds and non-arbitrarily.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which description best explains 'Public duty'?
options: a duty owed under public law that can support remedies such as mandamus
the principle under Article 310 that civil posts are held during the pleasure of the President or Governor, subject to constitutional safeguards
constitutional safeguards to specified civil servants against dismissal, removal or reduction in rank
questions.explanation: The existence of a public duty is central to mandamus.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Under the Legal Services Authorities framework, free legal services are targeted primarily at:
options: Statutorily specified eligible persons including certain disadvantaged categories and persons below notified income ceilings
Only senior citizens irrespective of means
Only accused persons in capital cases
questions.explanation: The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 specifies categories entitled to legal services and also permits income-based eligibility within prescribed limits.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which statement about judicial custody is correct?
options: The accused is kept in a police station as a matter of course
Police may interrogate without court permission
The accused is in custody under the authority of the magistrate, and police interrogation ordinarily requires court permission
Judicial custody and police custody are identical
questions.explanation: Judicial custody is custody under judicial authority, usually in jail; further police interrogation requires permission of the court.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which statement about parole in India is the most accurate?
options: Parole is an absolute constitutional right in every case
State Governments generally frame parole rules, and release depends on applicable law and conditions
questions.explanation: Parole is generally governed by State prison laws/rules and is not an unconditional right in every case.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which institution has statutory functions concerning standards of professional conduct and legal education for advocates?
options: Bar Council framework under the Advocates Act
questions.explanation: The Advocates Act, 1961 creates the Bar Council structure and assigns functions relating to the legal profession and legal education.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which statement is constitutionally correct regarding the size of the Union Council of Ministers?
options: It cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha, including the Prime Minister
It cannot exceed 10% of Rajya Sabha
The ceiling is fixed by the President annually
questions.explanation: Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, caps the total number of Ministers including the Prime Minister at 15% of Lok Sabha strength.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: The Tenth Schedule presently prescribes what fixed time limit for the presiding officer to decide a defection petition?
options: No express fixed time limit in the Schedule
questions.explanation: The Tenth Schedule does not prescribe a specific decision period, although courts have emphasised timely adjudication.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Who has constitutional power to punish for contempt of itself?
options: Supreme Court and High Courts as courts of record
questions.explanation: Articles 129 and 215 declare the Supreme Court and High Courts to be courts of record with power to punish for contempt.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: A key difference between the British and Indian constitutional systems is that:
options: The Indian Parliament is legally sovereign in the same sense as Westminster
Indian parliamentary legislation is subject to constitutional limitations and judicial review
British courts exercise Indian-style constitutional judicial review of Acts of Parliament
questions.explanation: India combines parliamentary government with a written supreme Constitution and judicial review; Parliament is not legally sovereign in the Westminster sense.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Which statement about sessions of Parliament is correct?
options: The Constitution mandates exactly three sessions every year
There must not be more than six months between two sessions
Parliament must meet at least 120 days each year
Only the Prime Minister may summon Parliament
questions.explanation: Article 85 requires that six months shall not intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next; the President summons Parliament.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: Article 142 is best understood as empowering the Supreme Court to:
options: Pass orders necessary for complete justice in causes or matters before it, subject to constitutional limits
questions.explanation: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass decrees or orders necessary for doing complete justice in matters before it, though the power remains constitutional in character.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Under UNCLOS, the maximum breadth of the territorial sea measured from the baseline is:
questions.explanation: UNCLOS permits a territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Under UNCLOS, the contiguous zone may extend up to:
questions.explanation: The contiguous zone may not extend beyond 24 nautical miles from the baselines.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The Exclusive Economic Zone under UNCLOS may extend up to:
questions.explanation: The EEZ shall not extend beyond 200 nautical miles from the relevant baselines.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: In the territorial sea, the coastal State principally exercises:
options: Sovereignty, subject to UNCLOS and other rules of international law
questions.explanation: Coastal State sovereignty extends to the territorial sea, air space above it, and bed and subsoil, subject to international law.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: In an EEZ, the coastal State has:
options: Full sovereignty identical to land territory
Sovereign rights over natural resources and specified jurisdiction, while other States retain certain freedoms
questions.explanation: The EEZ is a sui generis zone: coastal States have sovereign resource rights and specified jurisdiction, while other States retain navigation and overflight freedoms.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The normal baseline for measuring the territorial sea is generally:
options: The low-water line along the coast shown on officially recognised charts
The edge of the continental shelf
questions.explanation: UNCLOS Article 5 generally uses the low-water line as the normal baseline.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Innocent passage is a right principally associated with:
options: Foreign ships passing through the territorial sea
Aircraft overflying territorial sea without consent
questions.explanation: UNCLOS recognises innocent passage of ships through the territorial sea, subject to the Convention.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: A coastal State's continental shelf rights concern primarily:
options: The seabed and subsoil of submarine areas
questions.explanation: Continental shelf rights concern seabed and subsoil resources, not general sovereignty over the water column.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Where the continental margin does not reach 200 nautical miles, UNCLOS generally recognises a continental shelf to at least:
questions.explanation: Article 76 recognises the shelf to 200 nautical miles where the natural margin does not extend that far.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Freedom of the high seas includes, among other things:
options: A right to appropriate any seabed area as sovereign territory
A right to ignore anti-piracy rules
questions.explanation: High seas freedoms include navigation, overflight and other freedoms subject to UNCLOS.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Piracy under international law is classically subject to:
options: Exclusive territorial jurisdiction of the victim State only
questions.explanation: Piracy is a traditional basis for universal jurisdiction under international law.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The Area under UNCLOS refers broadly to:
options: The seabed and ocean floor beyond national jurisdiction
questions.explanation: UNCLOS treats the seabed beyond national jurisdiction as 'the Area'.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The regime of archipelagic waters is especially relevant to:
options: States constituted wholly by one or more archipelagos and possibly other islands
questions.explanation: UNCLOS creates a special archipelagic regime for qualifying archipelagic States.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: A coastal State in its EEZ must exercise its rights with:
options: Due regard to rights and duties of other States
questions.explanation: UNCLOS Article 56 requires due regard to the rights and duties of other States.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Other States in a coastal State's EEZ generally retain freedom of:
options: Navigation and overflight, subject to UNCLOS
questions.explanation: Article 58 preserves navigation, overflight and related freedoms for all States in the EEZ.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: How many principal organs of the United Nations are established by the Charter?
questions.explanation: The principal organs are the General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council, ICJ and Secretariat.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Which UN organ has primary responsibility for maintenance of international peace and security?
questions.explanation: The Security Council has primary responsibility for international peace and security under the UN Charter.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Article 51 of the UN Charter recognises:
options: The inherent right of individual or collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs
An unlimited right of humanitarian intervention
questions.explanation: Article 51 preserves individual or collective self-defence after an armed attack until the Security Council takes necessary measures.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: A substantive Security Council resolution generally requires:
options: A simple majority of all UN members
Nine affirmative votes including no veto by a permanent member, subject to Charter rules
questions.explanation: Under Article 27, substantive decisions require the prescribed majority and concurrence/no veto of permanent members, subject to abstention practice.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The ICJ is:
options: The principal judicial organ of the United Nations
questions.explanation: The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Contentious jurisdiction of the ICJ is principally based on:
options: Compulsory jurisdiction over every State automatically
questions.explanation: The ICJ's contentious jurisdiction depends on consent of States through relevant jurisdictional bases.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Who may be parties in contentious cases before the ICJ?
questions.explanation: Only States may be parties in contentious cases before the ICJ.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute refers to:
options: Sources/materials applied by the Court, including treaties, custom and general principles
questions.explanation: Article 38(1) lists conventions, international custom, general principles, and subsidiary means for determining rules of law.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Admission of a new UN member is decided by:
options: General Assembly upon recommendation of the Security Council
questions.explanation: Article 4 provides for admission by the General Assembly upon Security Council recommendation.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The UN General Assembly's ordinary resolutions are generally:
options: Legally binding on all States like treaties
Recommendations, except where the Charter gives internal legal effects such as budgetary or institutional decisions
questions.explanation: Most General Assembly resolutions are recommendatory, though some decisions have legal effect within the UN institutional framework.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Pacta sunt servanda means:
options: Treaties must be performed in good faith
All treaties are voidable at will
Domestic law always overrides treaty obligations
questions.explanation: The Vienna Convention expresses the rule that every treaty in force is binding and must be performed in good faith.
questions.reference: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Article 26

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: A State generally may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform a treaty under:
options: Pacta sunt servanda and the Vienna Convention framework
The doctrine of diplomatic protection only
questions.explanation: VCLT Article 27 generally bars reliance on internal law to justify treaty non-performance.
questions.reference: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Article 27

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: A reservation to a treaty is best described as:
options: A unilateral statement seeking to exclude or modify the legal effect of certain treaty provisions in their application to the reserving State
A diplomatic note terminating every treaty
questions.explanation: The VCLT defines a reservation as a unilateral statement purporting to exclude or modify certain treaty effects for that State.
questions.reference: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Article 2

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: A treaty is void if its conclusion was procured by the threat or use of force in violation of UN Charter principles under:
questions.explanation: The VCLT contains rules invalidating treaties procured by coercion involving unlawful force.
questions.reference: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Jus cogens refers to:
options: A peremptory norm of general international law from which no derogation is permitted
Only a Security Council press release
questions.explanation: Peremptory norms are norms accepted and recognised by the international community as non-derogable.
questions.reference: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Article 53

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The declaratory theory of recognition broadly holds that:
options: Recognition creates the State from nothing
Statehood primarily depends on objective conditions; recognition acknowledges an existing situation
questions.explanation: Under the declaratory view, recognition acknowledges rather than constitutes statehood.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The constitutive theory of recognition emphasises that:
options: Recognition by other States plays a constitutive role in international personality
questions.explanation: The constitutive theory gives recognition by existing States a central role in acquiring international personality.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The Montevideo formulation of statehood classically refers to:
options: Population, defined territory, government and capacity to enter relations
Only recognition by five permanent Security Council members
questions.explanation: The Montevideo criteria are permanent population, defined territory, government and capacity to enter into relations with other States.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: State succession concerns:
options: Replacement of one State by another in responsibility for international relations of territory
Election of a new government within the same State only
questions.explanation: State succession deals with changes in responsibility for international relations of territory.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: A dualist approach generally treats international and municipal law as:
options: Distinct legal systems requiring domestic transformation/incorporation for internal effect
questions.explanation: Dualism views the systems as distinct, with domestic incorporation often needed for municipal effect.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Territorial jurisdiction is primarily based on:
options: Conduct or consequences occurring within a State's territory
questions.explanation: Territoriality is the primary classical basis of criminal and regulatory jurisdiction.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The nationality principle permits a State, in appropriate cases, to regulate:
options: Conduct of its nationals even outside its territory
Only conduct on the high seas
questions.explanation: Nationality is a recognised basis of extraterritorial jurisdiction.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The passive personality principle bases jurisdiction principally on:
questions.explanation: Passive personality rests on the nationality of the victim.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The protective principle allows jurisdiction over certain foreign conduct threatening:
options: Vital security or governmental interests of the State
questions.explanation: The protective principle supports jurisdiction over foreign conduct directed against vital State interests.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Universal jurisdiction is most closely associated with offences considered of concern to the international community, classically including:
questions.explanation: Piracy is the classic example of universal jurisdiction.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Extradition is best described as:
options: Surrender by one State to another of a person sought for prosecution or punishment, pursuant to law/treaty
questions.explanation: Extradition is the formal surrender of a fugitive to another jurisdiction under applicable law or treaty.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The principle of speciality in extradition generally means:
options: The surrendered person should ordinarily be tried only for the offence(s) for which extradition was granted, subject to exceptions
Only political offences may be tried
questions.explanation: Speciality limits prosecution after extradition to the authorised offences unless applicable exceptions/consent apply.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Territorial asylum is granted by:
options: A State within its territory to a person seeking protection
questions.explanation: Territorial asylum concerns protection granted by a State within its territory.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Statelessness refers to a person who:
options: Is not considered a national by any State under the operation of its law
Lives outside the country of birth
questions.explanation: The 1954 Statelessness Convention uses this core definition.
questions.reference: 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Diplomatic protection generally involves a State invoking responsibility for injury to:
options: Its national by another State, subject to international-law conditions
Any corporation worldwide regardless of link
questions.explanation: Diplomatic protection is the invocation by a State of responsibility for injury to its national, subject to applicable rules.
questions.reference: International Law Commission articles on diplomatic protection

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The ICC's subject-matter jurisdiction under the Rome Statute covers:
options: Genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression
questions.explanation: Article 5 lists genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The ICC is designed to be:
options: A court of automatic first instance for all crimes
A replacement for every domestic criminal court
questions.explanation: The Rome Statute establishes complementarity: national systems have primary responsibility, subject to admissibility rules.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The ICC is seated in:
questions.explanation: The Rome Statute establishes the seat of the Court at The Hague, Netherlands.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The principle of distinction requires parties to an armed conflict to distinguish primarily between:
options: Civilians and combatants, and civilian objects and military objectives
questions.explanation: Distinction is a foundational IHL principle protecting civilians and civilian objects from direct attack.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The principle of proportionality in attack prohibits:
options: Any attack expected to cause incidental civilian harm excessive in relation to anticipated concrete and direct military advantage
questions.explanation: IHL proportionality prohibits excessive expected incidental civilian harm compared with anticipated military advantage.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: TRIPS is principally concerned with:
options: Trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights
questions.explanation: TRIPS sets multilateral minimum standards and disciplines concerning intellectual property in the WTO system.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The principle of Most-Favoured-Nation treatment in the WTO generally seeks to:
options: Prevent unjustified discrimination among trading partners regarding covered advantages
Require identical domestic taxes in all countries
questions.explanation: MFN generally requires an advantage granted to one WTO member to be extended to other members, subject to permitted exceptions.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The precautionary principle broadly supports:
options: Taking preventive action where there is a risk of serious environmental harm despite scientific uncertainty
Waiting for absolute certainty before any action
questions.explanation: The precautionary principle supports preventive measures even where scientific certainty is incomplete.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The 'polluter pays' principle means broadly that:
options: The polluter should bear the costs of pollution prevention and remediation rather than shifting them to society
questions.explanation: The principle allocates environmental costs to the polluter and is recognised in environmental governance.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The Paris Agreement primarily operates within the framework of:
options: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement is a treaty under the UNFCCC framework addressing climate change.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The expression mens rea most closely refers to:
options: A guilty mind or legally required mental element
questions.explanation: Mens rea denotes the mental element required for criminal liability, such as intention, knowledge, recklessness or negligence, depending on the offence.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Actus reus ordinarily refers to:
options: The external or conduct element of an offence
The motive for committing an offence
questions.explanation: Actus reus is the prohibited conduct, omission, circumstance or consequence constituting the external element of an offence.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: As a general rule, a motive is:
options: The same as intention in every offence
Relevant to explain conduct but distinct from the mental element of intention
questions.explanation: Motive is the reason why a person acts; intention concerns the result or conduct intended. Motive may be evidentially relevant but is not identical to mens rea.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: A mistake of fact may excuse criminal liability where the law so provides because it can:
options: Negate the required guilty mind or bring the act within a general exception
Convert every offence into a civil wrong
questions.explanation: A bona fide mistake of fact may negate mens rea or fall within a statutory general exception; mistake of law is ordinarily no excuse.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The maxim ignorantia juris non excusat means:
options: Ignorance of law is no excuse
Ignorance of fact is always an offence
Law must always be published in newspapers
Only judges are presumed to know law
questions.explanation: The general principle is that ignorance or mistake of law does not excuse criminal liability merely because the accused did not know the law.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The defence of insanity in criminal law principally focuses on:
options: The accused's legal capacity to understand the nature or wrongfulness of the act at the relevant time
Whether the accused later regretted the act
questions.explanation: The legal test concerns the accused's cognitive capacity at the time of the act, not merely the existence of a medical disorder.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Voluntary intoxication generally:
options: Does not by itself provide a blanket defence, though its effect may depend on the mental element required
questions.explanation: Voluntary intoxication is not a general excuse. Its relevance depends on the statutory rules and whether the required intention or knowledge is established.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The right of private defence is best described as:
options: A right of retaliation after danger has ended
A preventive right against certain unlawful aggression, subject to necessity and proportionality rules
A right available only to police
A right to punish a wrongdoer
questions.explanation: Private defence is preventive, not punitive. It operates against imminent unlawful aggression and is limited by statutory conditions.
questions.reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Right of Private Defence

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: An accident may exclude criminal liability when the act is:
options: Lawful, done in a lawful manner, with proper care and caution, and without criminal intention or knowledge
questions.explanation: The general exception for accident protects an unintended result of a lawful act lawfully done with proper care and caution.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Which stage ordinarily precedes an attempt?
questions.explanation: The usual sequence is intention, preparation, attempt and completion. Preparation is generally not punishable unless a statute specifically provides otherwise.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: An attempt becomes punishable principally because:
options: The accused has moved beyond mere preparation toward commission of the offence
The accused merely thought about the offence
The victim always suffers completed harm
questions.explanation: Attempt liability attaches when conduct crosses from preparation into a sufficiently proximate execution of the intended offence, subject to statutory formulation.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Abetment may broadly occur through:
options: Instigation, conspiracy accompanied by the required act/omission, or intentional aid
questions.explanation: Indian criminal law recognises abetment through instigation, specified conspiracy and intentional aid.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Criminal conspiracy is centrally based on:
options: An agreement between persons to do an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means, subject to statutory requirements
questions.explanation: The gravamen of conspiracy is the agreement to pursue the prohibited object or means; the precise requirement of an overt act depends on the statutory formulation.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Constructive or joint criminal liability may make a participant liable for acts done by others when:
options: The statutory conditions connecting the common intention/object and participation are satisfied
They live in the same city
questions.explanation: Joint liability doctrines depend on statutory elements such as common intention or common object; mere association is insufficient.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Strict liability in criminal law is exceptional because criminal offences ordinarily require:
options: A prohibited act plus the mental element specified by law
questions.explanation: Criminal liability usually requires both an external element and the prescribed mental element, although legislatures can create strict-liability offences.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Culpable homicide and murder are best understood as:
options: Related categories, with murder being the more aggravated form of culpable homicide under the statutory scheme
questions.explanation: The homicide provisions distinguish culpable homicide from its aggravated form, murder, through the statutory mental elements and exceptions.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, punishment for murder is contained in:
questions.explanation: Section 103 of the BNS provides punishment for murder.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder is contained in:
questions.explanation: Section 105 of the BNS deals with punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Grievous hurt differs from simple hurt because:
options: The law specifies particular aggravated kinds of bodily injury as grievous
Every bodily pain is automatically grievous
questions.explanation: The criminal code enumerates specified serious injuries as grievous hurt; other bodily pain, disease or infirmity may amount to hurt without necessarily being grievous.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Wrongful restraint principally involves:
options: Voluntarily obstructing a person so as to prevent movement in a direction in which that person has a right to proceed
questions.explanation: Wrongful restraint protects freedom of movement against unlawful obstruction.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Wrongful confinement is an aggravated form of restraint because the person is:
options: Prevented from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits
questions.explanation: Confinement involves total restraint within circumscribed limits rather than obstruction in only one direction.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Abduction generally requires:
options: Compelling or inducing a person by force or deceitful means to go from any place
Only taking a minor from a guardian
questions.explanation: Abduction focuses on movement caused by force or deceitful means, unlike forms of kidnapping that may hinge on age/guardianship or removal from India.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Consent in sexual-offence law is best understood as:
options: An unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated by words, gestures or other verbal/non-verbal communication, subject to statutory rules
questions.explanation: Modern statutory consent focuses on an unequivocal voluntary agreement; prior intimacy or lack of physical resistance does not by itself establish consent.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The essential idea of theft is dishonest moving of:
options: Movable property out of another person's possession without consent
Only money deposited in a bank
questions.explanation: Theft concerns dishonest taking/moving of movable property out of another's possession without consent.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, theft is defined/punished in the provision beginning at:
questions.explanation: Section 303 is the BNS theft provision.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Extortion differs from theft because extortion typically involves:
options: Putting a person in fear of injury and thereby dishonestly inducing delivery of property or valuable security
Secret moving of property without the possessor's consent
questions.explanation: Extortion uses fear of injury to induce delivery; theft involves taking movable property without consent.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Robbery may arise from aggravated forms of:
questions.explanation: Robbery is an aggravated form of theft or extortion involving specified violence, fear or immediacy conditions.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, robbery is dealt with in:
questions.explanation: Section 309 of the BNS deals with robbery.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Dacoity requires the conjoint commission or attempt of robbery by at least:
questions.explanation: Dacoity is robbery committed or attempted conjointly by five or more persons, including persons present and aiding.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, dacoity is dealt with in:
questions.explanation: Section 310 of the BNS deals with dacoity.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Criminal breach of trust centrally requires:
options: Entrustment or dominion over property followed by dishonest misappropriation/use/disposal contrary to law or contract
Taking property without prior possession or entrustment in every case
questions.explanation: Entrustment is a defining feature of criminal breach of trust; dishonest dealing with entrusted property distinguishes it from a mere civil breach.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Cheating generally involves:
options: Deception that dishonestly or fraudulently induces delivery/retention of property or induces an act/omission causing or likely to cause harm
Mere failure to perform every promise
questions.explanation: Cheating requires deception plus the statutorily specified inducement and consequence; a later breach of contract alone does not automatically establish initial dishonest intent.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Mischief primarily protects against:
options: Intentional or knowing wrongful loss or damage through destruction or change in property/value/utility
questions.explanation: Mischief concerns causing wrongful loss or damage by destroying property or changing it so as to diminish value or utility, subject to statutory wording.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Criminal trespass requires entry into or unlawful remaining on property with specified criminal intent, such as intent to:
options: Commit an offence or intimidate, insult or annoy the possessor
questions.explanation: Criminal trespass is not mere unauthorized entry; the statutory intent element is crucial.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Criminal defamation is principally concerned with:
options: Making or publishing an imputation concerning a person with the requisite intention/knowledge and resulting reputational harm, subject to exceptions
questions.explanation: The offence protects reputation against specified imputations while preserving statutory exceptions such as certain good-faith/public-interest communications.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: An unlawful assembly is based on:
options: A statutory minimum number of persons sharing one of the specified common objects
questions.explanation: The offence turns on the statutory minimum and a common object falling within the enumerated unlawful objects, not mere gathering.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force substantially on:
questions.explanation: The Central Government appointed 1 July 2024 as the date on which the BNS came into force, with the notified exception relating to the hit-and-run sub-section.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Which of the following is expressly included among punishments under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
options: Disqualification from voting in every case
questions.explanation: The BNS expressly recognises community service as one of the punishments that may be imposed where the Code so provides.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: For purposes of the BNS, a 'child' means a person below the age of:
questions.explanation: The BNS defines 'child' as a person below eighteen years of age.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The BNS can apply to certain offences committed outside India when the offence targets:
options: A computer resource located in India
questions.explanation: The BNS contains extra-territorial provisions including specified offences committed outside India targeting a computer resource located in India.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Which newer offence is expressly recognised in the BNS as a distinct property offence?
questions.explanation: The BNS expressly recognises snatching as a distinct offence, unlike the IPC's older structure.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The BNS expressly introduces provisions dealing with:
options: Organised crime and petty organised crime
Only breach of trust by trustees under civil law
questions.explanation: The BNS specifically codifies organised crime and petty organised crime offences.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The BNS contains a specific offence addressing a terrorist act within the general penal code itself. This statement is:
options: Incorrect, terrorism can never appear in a general penal code
Incorrect, BNS applies only to civil disputes
questions.explanation: The BNS contains a specific provision on terrorist acts, while special anti-terror legislation such as UAPA also continues to operate according to law.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The IPC-era offence of sedition was not reproduced under the same label in the BNS. Instead, the BNS addresses certain acts endangering:
options: Sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
questions.explanation: The BNS uses a differently framed offence concerning acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India rather than reproducing IPC Section 124A under the old sedition label.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Which statement best reflects the treatment of group murder on specified identity grounds under the BNS?
options: The BNS expressly provides aggravated treatment for murder by a group of five or more persons acting in concert on specified grounds
The BNS abolishes murder liability for groups
The provision applies only to corporations
questions.explanation: The BNS includes an aggravated group-murder provision where five or more persons acting in concert commit murder on specified identity-related grounds.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: A person can be liable for an offence committed beyond India under the BNS when Indian law makes that person liable to be tried in India. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: The BNS preserves extra-territorial reach in specified circumstances, including persons liable under Indian law for offences committed outside India.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 principally replaces the:
questions.explanation: The BNSS is the principal criminal procedure code that replaced the CrPC, 1973 from 1 July 2024, subject to transition provisions.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 principally replaces the:
questions.explanation: The BSA is the current general law of evidence replacing the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 from 1 July 2024, subject to savings/transition provisions.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Information relating to a cognizable offence under the BNSS may, subject to the statutory framework, be given:
questions.explanation: The BNSS expressly accommodates information by electronic communication, alongside oral information, subject to prescribed authentication/recording requirements.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: A cognizable offence is one in which police may ordinarily:
options: Arrest without warrant in accordance with law and investigate without a magistrate's order as permitted by the Code
questions.explanation: Cognizable classification carries statutory police powers to investigate and, subject to safeguards, arrest without warrant.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: A non-cognizable case ordinarily requires police to obtain an order from the competent Magistrate before:
questions.explanation: The criminal procedure framework generally requires a Magistrate's order for investigation of non-cognizable offences.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Bail is best understood as:
options: Conditional release from custody subject to appearance and other lawful conditions
A declaration that no offence occurred
questions.explanation: Bail regulates pre-trial or pending-proceeding liberty; it does not amount to acquittal or determination of innocence.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The BNSS expands use of audio-video electronic means in criminal process. This is intended principally to:
options: Enable specified procedural acts to be conducted/recorded electronically while preserving statutory safeguards
questions.explanation: The BNSS expressly contemplates electronic/audio-video modes for a range of procedural steps while retaining legal safeguards.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: For offences punishable with seven years or more, the BNSS strengthens the role of:
options: Forensic investigation/forensic experts, subject to statutory implementation
questions.explanation: The BNSS introduces an enhanced forensic-investigation requirement for serious offences, subject to statutory conditions and implementation arrangements.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Under the BSA, electronic or digital records are:
options: Recognised within the law of evidence subject to statutory conditions
questions.explanation: The BSA expressly integrates electronic and digital records into the evidentiary framework, subject to authenticity/admissibility requirements.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The burden of proof generally lies on the person who:
options: Asserts facts necessary to establish the legal right or liability claimed, subject to statutory presumptions
questions.explanation: The general evidentiary rule places the burden on the party who would fail if the asserted facts were not proved, subject to specific presumptions and exceptions.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 primarily addresses corruption involving:
options: Public servants and associated bribery-related conduct
questions.explanation: The PCA creates offences relating to bribery and corruption involving public servants and related participants.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Under the Prevention of Corruption Act, the modern statutory expression commonly used for the benefit involved in bribery is:
questions.explanation: Amendments to the PCA use the expression 'undue advantage' in the bribery framework.
questions.reference: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, as amended

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 is closely connected with enforcement of the constitutional abolition of:
questions.explanation: The Act provides penal consequences for practices arising from untouchability, complementing Article 17 of the Constitution.
questions.reference: Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; Constitution, Article 17

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Plea bargaining in Indian criminal procedure is:
options: A statutory mechanism available for specified cases subject to exclusions and court supervision
A private settlement that automatically ends every prosecution
Available for every offence including all serious offences without restriction
questions.explanation: Indian criminal procedure recognises plea bargaining for specified offences/cases with statutory exclusions, safeguards and judicial oversight.
questions.reference: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 - plea bargaining

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: A central policy objective of plea bargaining is to:
options: Facilitate negotiated disposition of eligible criminal cases while retaining statutory safeguards
Replace criminal law with contract law
questions.explanation: Plea bargaining seeks efficient resolution of eligible cases through a supervised process rather than abolishing judicial control.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: A prosecution for corruption is not converted into a purely civil dispute merely because money is involved because:
options: The statute protects public integrity and criminalises specified corrupt conduct
Civil courts have no jurisdiction anywhere
questions.explanation: Corruption offences protect public administration and integrity; their criminal character comes from statutory elements, not merely the presence of money.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The presumption of innocence most directly means that:
options: The prosecution ordinarily bears the burden of proving guilt according to the applicable standard, subject to valid statutory presumptions
The accused can never be arrested
questions.explanation: Presumption of innocence places the primary burden on the prosecution, though legislation may create constitutionally valid presumptions for particular facts/offences.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The criminal standard 'beyond reasonable doubt' principally applies to:
options: Proof of guilt by the prosecution, subject to the legal allocation of particular burdens
questions.explanation: A criminal conviction ordinarily requires proof of guilt beyond reasonable doubt, while particular defences or statutory presumptions may allocate different burdens.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Double jeopardy protects against:
options: Repeated prosecution/punishment for the same offence within the scope of the constitutional/statutory rules
Civil and criminal proceedings in all circumstances
questions.explanation: Article 20(2) and criminal procedure protections prevent repeated prosecution/punishment for the same offence within their respective legal scope.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The privilege against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) is available to:
options: A person accused of an offence against being compelled to be a witness against oneself
Every witness against answering any question whatsoever
questions.explanation: Article 20(3) protects an accused person against compelled testimonial self-incrimination, subject to the distinction between testimonial and physical evidence.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Consent is not a defence in every criminal case because:
options: The law may treat some harms or circumstances as incapable of being legally justified by consent
questions.explanation: Consent operates only within statutory limits. The law may withhold the defence for specified harms, ages, relationships or public-policy reasons.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Necessity as a general criminal-law idea is most closely associated with:
options: Choosing conduct to prevent a greater imminent harm under narrowly defined legal conditions
questions.explanation: Necessity-type provisions excuse narrowly defined conduct undertaken to prevent greater harm; they do not authorise retaliation.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Common intention and common object are:
options: Distinct statutory bases of group liability with different elements
questions.explanation: Indian criminal law distinguishes liability based on common intention from unlawful-assembly/common-object liability; their statutory elements differ.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The distinction between intention and knowledge is important in homicide law because:
options: Different mental states can affect whether conduct amounts to murder, culpable homicide or another offence
questions.explanation: Homicide classification depends significantly on the particular intention or knowledge proved, together with statutory circumstances and exceptions.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: The presence of entrustment most strongly points toward which offence rather than theft?
questions.explanation: Criminal breach of trust is built around property entrusted to the accused or over which the accused has dominion, followed by dishonest misuse.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: An FIR is primarily associated with information relating to:
options: A decree in a civil suit
questions.explanation: The first-information mechanism in criminal procedure concerns information relating to cognizable offences and triggers the statutory police process.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: A confession caused by an inducement, threat, coercion or promise from a person in authority may be:
options: Excluded or treated as irrelevant under the statutory confession rules
Admissible merely because it is written
questions.explanation: The evidentiary law imposes safeguards against confessions obtained by prohibited inducement, threat, coercion or promise.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: A fact forming part of the same transaction may be relevant even if it occurred at a different time or place. This principle is commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: Facts forming part of the same transaction may be relevant because their connection makes them part of the transaction under the statutory relevance rule.

questions.subject: Law of Crimes
questions.question: Leading questions are ordinarily most freely permitted during:
options: Examination-in-chief without permission in every case
questions.explanation: Evidence law generally permits leading questions in cross-examination, while restricting them in examination-in-chief and re-examination except in specified circumstances or with permission.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: The maxim ubi jus ibi remedium means:
options: Where there is a right, there is a remedy
No one should be judge in own cause
An act of court shall prejudice no one
questions.explanation: The maxim expresses the general idea that a legal right ordinarily carries a legal remedy when infringed.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: Damnum sine injuria refers to:
options: Damage without infringement of a legal right
Infringement of a legal right without actual damage
Damage caused by a crime only
questions.explanation: Damnum sine injuria is actual loss or damage without violation of a legal right and is ordinarily not actionable in tort merely because loss occurred.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: Injuria sine damno refers to:
options: Violation of a legal right without proof of actual damage
questions.explanation: Where an absolute/private legal right is infringed, an action may lie even without proof of measurable loss.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: Volenti non fit injuria is based on:
options: Free and informed consent to the relevant risk
questions.explanation: The defence applies where the claimant freely and knowingly agreed to run the particular risk, subject to limits imposed by law and public policy.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: Contributory negligence concerns:
options: The claimant's own lack of reasonable care contributing to the damage
